title: When the Language Breaks
premise: Oscar Nystrom, a retired court stenographer who writes postcards to her childhood home—burned down decades ago in a fire the family never discusses—has spent her life transcribing other people's words while keeping her own unsaid. When demolition of the old neighborhood forces a final clearing-out, she finds a box of undelivered letters behind a wardrobe: letters her mother wrote to Oscar's disappeared brother, and one letter addressed to Oscar herself, never sent. Reading them, she learns the fire was no accident and that her silence was purchased, not chosen. The novel ends with Oscar testifying—not in a courtroom, but at a community hearing on the neighborhood's redevelopment—finally speaking the family's secret aloud, then mailing one last postcard to the burned address, addressed this time to herself.
about_author: Ada Dunmore is the pen name of a former legal transcriptionist who spent twenty years listening to testimony in small-town courthouses across the upper Midwest. She writes about the people whose truths never made it into the record.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Oscar, in her own close third-person POV, catalogs her apartment with the same precision she once used for court transcripts, revealing her habit of writing weekly postcards to an address that no longer exists. She introduces her ritual of 'the unsaid list'—things she'll tell her brother when he returns. Emotional beat: tender, controlled loneliness masking dread.

chapters.title: Notice of Demolition
chapters.summary: A city notice arrives: the old neighborhood's last standing block, including the charred lot of her childhood home, will be cleared for a transit hub. Her sister Vera calls, brisk and deflecting, insisting there's nothing left to salvage. Oscar decides to go anyway. Emotional beat: quiet alarm; the past acquiring an expiration date.

chapters.title: What Vera Kept
chapters.summary: Vera's POV reveals she has known about the demolition for months and has been quietly paying a neighbor to watch the property—because she knows what's still inside it. Flashbacks show the sisters' divergent survival strategies after the fire: Vera through control, Oscar through disappearance. Emotional beat: guilt dressed as competence.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Back in Oscar's POV, she searches the ruined house before the crews arrive and pries loose a panel behind her mother's wardrobe, finding a tin box: dozens of undelivered letters in her mother's hand, all addressed to her missing brother Elias—and one sealed envelope with Oscar's name. She cannot open that one yet. Emotional beat: vertigo; the floor of her identity giving way.

chapters.title: Letters to a Ghost
chapters.summary: Over several nights Oscar reads her mother's letters, which trace Elias's slow estrangement, his accusations about their father's debts, and a growing fear that 'he knows what happened in the shop.' The letters stop mid-sentence two weeks before the fire. Emotional beat: mounting dread as the official story begins to crack.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed the Report
chapters.summary: Oscar tracks down Halvorsen, the retired fire investigator whose report blamed faulty wiring. He is dying, unguarded, and admits the wiring finding was 'arranged'—a favor to someone with money in the block. He won't say who. Emotional beat: the sickening confirmation that justice was traded away, and that her family may have been both victim and party to it.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: In Vera's POV, Oscar brings the letters home. Vera finally confesses: their father started the fire himself—for insurance—to erase evidence of the debts, and Elias left because he threatened to go to the police; the family let him go and let him be blamed by rumor. Their mother wrote letters she never had the courage to send. Emotional beat: the climax of secrets; rage, grief, and the shattering of the sisters' unspoken contract of silence.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Alone, Oscar opens the letter addressed to her. Her mother writes that she saw Oscar watching the fire from the bus stop that night—that Oscar knew, or sensed, something—and begs forgiveness for teaching her daughter that silence was safety. Oscar realizes her whole life of transcription and invisibility was built on that night. Emotional beat: devastating self-recognition.

chapters.title: Public Record
chapters.summary: At the city's final community hearing on the redevelopment, residents give statements. Oscar takes the microphone, identifies herself as a former stenographer, and reads her mother's last unfinished letter into the record—the fire, the insurance, Elias's flight—refusing the comfort of anonymity. Some neighbors are furious; others begin telling their own buried truths. Emotional beat: catharsis; speech as an act of justice outside any court.

chapters.title: Return Address
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Oscar and Vera visit Elias, now living under another name two states away; he listens, does not forgive fully, but asks for copies of their mother's letters—a beginning. Oscar writes one final postcard to the burned address, but addresses it to herself, listing what she has said instead of what she hasn't. Emotional beat: hard-won belonging; identity rebuilt through voice rather than silence.
